title: Communication-efficient Federated Graph Classification via Generative Diffusion Modeling

problem.claim: Federated GNNs face high communication overhead from repeated parameter exchanges and non-IID data across clients.

gap.claim: The abstract identifies the need for an FGNN approach that reduces communication while handling non-IID client data.

contributions.claim: CeFGC is an FGNN paradigm that limits server-client communication to three rounds for training over non-IID data.
CeFGC uses client-trained generative diffusion models, server redistribution, synthetic graph generation, local GNN training, and final model-weight aggregation.
The work analyzes the I/O complexity of communication volume for CeFGC.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe CeFGC as a novel FGNN paradigm.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the theoretical analysis shows CeFGC requires only a constant three communication rounds.
The authors report that extensive experiments on several real graph datasets demonstrate CeFGC's effectiveness and efficiency against state-of-the-art competitors.
The authors report superior performance on non-IID graphs, attributing it to alignment of local and global model objectives and enrichment of the training set with diverse graphs.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNNs are effective for learning from graph-structured data, and FGNNs support distributed GNN training over decentralized data.
FGNNs face repeated communication overhead and non-IID data across clients.
CeFGC limits communication to three rounds and uses generative diffusion models to represent local graph distributions, generate synthetic graphs, train local GNNs, and aggregate model weights.
The authors analyze the I/O complexity of CeFGC's communication volume.
Experiments on several real graph datasets compare CeFGC with state-of-the-art competitors and report effectiveness, efficiency, and performance on non-IID graphs.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the real graph datasets, evaluation metrics, or competitor names.
The abstract does not provide numerical performance results or detailed I/O complexity bounds.
The abstract does not describe privacy guarantees, convergence conditions, or the quality of generated graphs.
